article.title: The election model is a little too popular
article.subtitle: Getting meta about my plans for 2024.

extraction.summary: Silver discusses his uncertainty about how, or whether, to publish an election model for 2024 after leaving FiveThirtyEight and Disney. He notes that he still owns the model's intellectual property. His argument is that the 538 forecast became so popular that he lost control of how it was interpreted: readers filtered the probabilities through partisanship and stress, and sometimes confused his model with others. The options he weighs are a paywall, a different audience (business, tech, forecasting or gambling), a deliberately low-fi version updated once or twice a week with probabilities rounded to 5 percent, or licensing or selling the model privately for financial hedging. The article contains almost no model mechanics; its value is mainly in forecast communication and evaluation.

findings.statement: Silver argues that public misreading of probabilistic election forecasts is not mainly a matter of people failing to understand probability or rounding 70 percent up to 100 percent. In his view, readers interpret forecasts in many different ways, and those interpretations are mediated by partisanship and election-related stress.

quantities.name: probability allegedly rounded up
quantities.context: the popular claim that people round 70 percent to 100 percent, which Silver says lacks empirical support

findings.rationale: Silver says there is not much empirical evidence that people round 70 percent up to 100 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s actually not much empirical evidence for the latter claim
findings.europe_note: European forecasters should expect partisan-motivated readings of their probabilities, and these will vary by party camp.

findings.statement: Silver estimates that among FiveThirtyEight forecast readers, about 10 wanted reassurance that their candidate would win for every 1 who was interested in forecasting as an intellectual exercise.

quantities.name: ratio of reassurance-seeking readers to forecasting-interested readers
quantities.context: Silver's rough estimate for the 538 audience

findings.evidence_quote: there were probably 10 who just wanted reassurance that their guy was going to win
findings.europe_note: Audience composition should shape how forecasts are framed and presented.

findings.statement: When a forecast reaches mass scale (538's 2016 forecast was seen by tens of millions of people and was, according to Chartbeat, the most engaging content on the English-speaking internet), the forecaster loses control of the narrative. Far more people see the headline numbers than read the written context around them.
findings.rationale: Headline probabilities spread much further than the analysis that explains them.
findings.evidence_quote: far more people saw the numbers than read my careful contextualizations about them
findings.europe_note: Put the key uncertainty framing in the headline number display itself, not only in the accompanying text.

findings.statement: Readers form impressions of a forecast from media coverage elsewhere and from what other people tell them. They also misattribute other models' results to a given model; for example, Silver is still sent screenshots of the Upshot's 2016 banner headline.
findings.evidence_quote: people may misattribute results they see from a different model to mine
findings.europe_note: Clear branding helps distinguish a model from other forecasts and seat projections.

findings.statement: Silver says the FiveThirtyEight model departed from the consensus in two notable years. In 2016 it was much more bullish on Trump than the consensus. In 2022 it was somewhat more bullish on Democrats than the consensus.
findings.rationale: These examples show the model often got lumped in with other coverage even though it bucked that coverage.
findings.evidence_quote: Our model was much more bullish on Trump than the consensus in 2016 and somewhat more bullish on Democrats than the consensus in 2022.
findings.europe_note: Evaluate a model against consensus benchmarks, not only against outcomes.

findings.statement: Silver holds that a forecasting model should be judged by its long-term documented calibration and accuracy record, not by partisan narratives about individual elections. He says 538's models have a long, well-documented record of strong calibration and accuracy.
findings.rationale: Partisan narratives about the models are detached from their actual track record.
findings.evidence_quote: completely detached from their long, well-documented track record of strong calibration and accuracy
findings.europe_note: Publish calibration records across many races and countries.

findings.statement: Silver defends probabilistic election forecasting as one of the fundamental ways to test whether one's view of the world is accurate. He considers most critiques of such forecasting ill-considered.
findings.rationale: Journalists ought to be concerned with accuracy.
findings.evidence_quote: forecasting is one of the fundamental ways to test whether your view of the world is accurate

findings.statement: Silver considered a deliberately low-fi version of the forecast. It would be published once or twice a week rather than updated around the clock, with probabilities rounded to the nearest 5 percent and simple, non-immersive graphics.
findings.rationale: The aim is a healthier relationship between readers and the forecast, avoiding compulsive refreshing and false precision.
findings.evidence_quote: Maybe we’d round probabilities to the nearest 5 percent.
findings.europe_note: Coarse rounding and less frequent updates suit noisy multiparty polling environments.

findings.statement: Silver suggests that hedging financial risk may be a better use case for election forecasts than informing voters. Whether a candidate's chance is 30, 50 or 70 percent matters little to a voter's decision but is directly relevant to calculated financial decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: People use election forecasts to hedge financial risk and to make other sorts of bets.
findings.europe_note: Probabilities of specific coalition outcomes are valuable to financial users.

findings.statement: Silver weighed putting the forecast behind a paywall, or targeting a business, tech, economics or forecasting/gambling audience instead of politics junkies. His reasoning is that a more self-selected audience would interpret the model better.
findings.rationale: A self-selected audience is less driven by partisan reassurance-seeking.
findings.evidence_quote: putting the numbers behind a paywall might help a lot to draw a more self-selected audience

findings.statement: Silver retains the intellectual property of the FiveThirtyEight election model after his split with Disney. As of September 2023, he had not decided how to deploy it for 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: I still retain that intellectual property even after my split with Disney.

political_insights.insight: As of September 2023, Silver saw a Trump-Biden rematch as likely, with possibly neither primary competitive. He expected a potentially very close election lasting another 14 months, with few new day-to-day storylines.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: A long, stable rematch campaign may mean low poll volatility while public attention to every small shift stays intense.

political_insights.insight: Silver says arguments about polling reliability and forecasting are filtered through a partisan lens, and that elections involving Trump make these issues worse.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Expect polling accuracy debates to be politicized, especially around populist candidates.

references.description: Silver's earlier post about steeling yourself for a long 2024 election year
Chartbeat ranking of the 538 2016 forecast as the most engaging content on the English-speaking internet
538 calibration and accuracy track record ('long, well-documented track record of strong calibration and accuracy')
Planned future Silver Bulletin post on evidence about people rounding 70 percent probabilities to 100 percent

open_questions: What empirical evidence does Silver have on how people perceive probabilities such as 70 percent (promised in a future post)?
Which publication format did the 2024 Silver Bulletin model ultimately adopt?
Where is 538's documented calibration analysis, and what does it show?
